opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think scaling is really the central question for us, and there are a few different axes along which we think about it.

The first one is sample efficiency. A lot of the earlier work in this space, AlphaEvolve and FunSearch for example, relied on thousands or even tens of thousands of program evaluations to get to strong results. That's fine if you're Google and you have an enormous compute budget, but it makes this kind of approach inaccessible to most researchers. So with Shinka Evolve, a big part of the design philosophy was: how do we get to good solutions with far fewer samples? We introduced things like novelty-based rejection sampling, where we embed candidate programs and, if a proposed mutation is too similar to something we've already seen, we ask an LLM to judge whether it's actually meaningfully new before we spend compute evaluating it. That alone filters out a lot of wasted evaluations.

The second piece is parent selection and balancing exploration with exploitation. We use an island model with a population archive, and we sample parents in a way that weights both fitness and how many offspring a program has already produced. So you don't just keep hammering on the current best solution; you keep some diversity alive, which matters a lot once you scale up the number of generations.

Third, and I think this is underrated, is the ensemble of LLMs itself. Rather than committing to one frontier model, we treat model selection as a bandit problem. Different models are good at different kinds of mutations at different stages of the search, so we adaptively shift our sampling budget toward whichever model is currently producing the most improvement. That gives you a kind of automatic scaling with the model ecosystem: as new models come out, you just drop them into the pool.

And then looking forward, I think the really exciting scaling direction is moving from a fixed task to more open-ended settings. Right now you still need a human to specify the evaluation function. The next step is getting systems that can propose their own problems, build up a library of reusable insights across runs, sort of meta-learning the scratchpad of what worked, and transfer that across tasks. That's where I think you get compounding returns rather than just throwing more compute at a single optimization problem.

So in short: be smarter about which programs you evaluate, keep diversity in the population, adaptively use the right models, and ultimately close the loop so the system accumulates knowledge over time.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is the question we think about constantly, because the naive version of LLM-driven evolution is embarrassingly wasteful. You sample a program, you run it, you score it, you throw most of it away. And every one of those samples is an expensive LLM call plus an expensive evaluation. So when people say "scale," my first reaction is actually: scale what? More samples is the obvious lever, but it's also the least interesting one. The interesting levers are about getting more information out of each sample.

The first thing that mattered enormously for us was sample efficiency on the search side, which sounds boring but is where most of the gains came from. In ShinkaEvolve the whole design philosophy was: AlphaEvolve-style systems were burning thousands of evaluations on problems like circle packing, and we wanted to get there in a few hundred. The way you do that is you stop treating the archive as a flat population. We sample parents with a mix of fitness-weighted and novelty-weighted selection, we keep islands so you don't collapse to one basin early, and crucially we have this rejection step before you even evaluate: an embedding-based novelty filter. If the LLM proposes a program that's basically a cosmetic rewrite of something already in the archive, you don't pay to run it. That alone kills a huge fraction of the wasted compute, because LLMs love to propose the same three ideas over and over.

The second lever is the LLM ensemble, and I think this is underappreciated. We don't commit to one model. We treat the choice of which LLM to query as a bandit problem. Different models have different "styles" of mutation. Some are good at bold architectural rewrites, some are good at careful local tweaks, and which one is useful changes over the course of the run. Early on you want exploration, later you want refinement. So you adaptively shift sampling probabilities toward whichever model has been producing improvements recently. That makes the system robust to scaling up the number of models without you having to hand-tune anything, and it means a cheaper model can carry most of the load with the expensive model only being called when it's actually paying off.

Then there's the question of what you're actually mutating. One of the mistakes I think people make is asking the LLM to rewrite the entire program every time. That scales terribly, the context gets huge, and the model tends to regress things that were working. We lean on diff-based edits and let the user mark which regions of the code are mutable. That's a bit of inductive bias, but it means the search space is sane and each sample is cheap in tokens.

Now, the harder scaling question, the one I don't think anyone has fully solved, is scaling across problems rather than within a problem. Right now every run starts from scratch. You learn nothing from the thousand programs you evolved yesterday on a different task. The thing I'm most excited about is closing that loop: using the trajectories of successful evolutionary runs as training data, so the proposal distribution itself improves. Then the LLM isn't just a fixed mutation operator, it's something that's getting better at being a mutation operator. That's where I think this stops being "clever search around a frozen model" and becomes an actual open-ended system.

And honestly, the last thing I'd say is that evaluation is the real bottleneck, not the LLM. On the math problems evaluation is cheap, so you can be sloppy. But when we did things like evolving mixture-of-experts load balancing losses, or the AtCoder heuristic contest stuff, each evaluation is a real training run or a real simulation. There, scaling means being smart about cheap proxy evaluations, early stopping on obviously bad candidates, and parallelizing the evaluation across machines, because the LLM calls are almost free by comparison. So the honest answer is: it depends what regime you're in, and a good system should be able to notice which regime it's in and reallocate accordingly.

r002.rationale: It says model usefulness changes over the run and sampling probabilities shift based on recent improvements, but does not link the best model choice to the parent program.

r003.rationale: It describes using a bandit to adapt model sampling probabilities over the course of a run while programs are being evolved.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish doing more search from getting more out of each attempt. You can give an LLM more calls and generate more candidate programs, but if they’re all variations on the same idea, you’re not necessarily making much progress.

So I’d think about the whole loop: which programs you select as parents, what information you give the model, and how you evaluate its proposals. The feedback needs to help the next attempt. Did the program fail to execute? Did it produce an incorrect result? Or was it correct but slower? Those are very different signals.

Then there’s the allocation of compute. You want to explore different approaches, but you also want to spend more effort on promising ones. And you need to preserve some diversity, because an approach that looks weaker initially might open up a much better direction later.

Parallelism can help with throughput, but I’d measure scaling in terms of improvement per unit of total compute, including evaluation. Ultimately, the question is: as we spend more, does the system keep finding meaningfully better programs, or does it just keep sampling around the same solution?

r002.rationale: It mentions choosing parent programs, but does not state that the best LLM for proposing an improvement can vary by parent.

r003.rationale: It discusses allocating compute, exploration, and diversity, but does not state that Shinka Evolve adapts its evolutionary search algorithm during a program-optimization run.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to make the search more sample efficient, rather than just throwing more LLM calls at it. You have this loop where you propose a change to a program, evaluate it, and use the feedback to decide what to try next. So the question is: how much useful progress do you get per unit of compute?

There are a few decisions in that loop that really matter. Which programs do you select as parents? What context do you give the model? And which model do you use for a particular mutation? You can treat those as adaptive decisions: spend more resources on strategies that are producing improvements, while retaining enough exploration to discover something different.

Evaluation is also crucial. If you can reject an invalid or clearly unpromising candidate cheaply, you can reserve expensive evaluations for the interesting ones. And you want to preserve diversity, because if every worker is modifying essentially the same solution, parallelism doesn't buy you very much.

So I would think about scaling the whole system—the proposal mechanism, the evaluation pipeline, and the allocation of compute—rather than assuming that a bigger model or a larger population will automatically give you better results.

r003.rationale: It describes making search decisions adaptive during the proposal-and-evaluation loop, allocating more resources to strategies producing improvements while optimizing programs.
